concepts.label: Courtship
concepts.gloss: The use of suasive devices for transcending social estrangement; rhetoric generated wherever beings of different social kinds communicate across the mystery of hierarchic difference. Not primarily sexual but structural.

concepts.label: Mystery (social)
concepts.gloss: The quasi-magical opacity that attaches to hierarchic difference and makes it suasively potent. Embarrassment, glamour, military caste, and the aura of office are its variants.

concepts.label: Hierarchy
concepts.gloss: The ordered gradation of social kinds that generates conditions for courtship. Any division of labor produces occupational classes and thereby the conditions for courtly intercourse between them.

concepts.label: Identification across ranks
concepts.gloss: The aim and product of courtship: suasive address that provisionally closes the distance between unequal social kinds. Socioanagogic reading detects implicit identifications between social and cosmic orders.

concepts.label: Consubstantiality (implicit)
concepts.gloss: Not named directly but operative: estranged parties are already bound by common participation in the hierarchic order, enabling identification despite rank difference. The ground of rhetorical convertibility.

concepts.label: Socioanagogic interpretation
concepts.gloss: Secular adaptation of the medieval anagogical sense: reading social hierarchy where divine or erotic imagery appears on the surface. Positioned midway between Marx's rage at mystification and Carlyle's adulation of mystery.

concepts.label: Embarrassment (social)
concepts.gloss: Involuntary self-constraint triggered by hierarchic difference; evidence of mystery in social intercourse. A non-deliberate rhetorical effect — the sign of different social kinds in contact.

concepts.label: Glamour
concepts.gloss: Corruption of 'gramarye' (necromancy, magic): 'any artificial interest in, or association with, an object, through which it appears elusively magnified or glorified.' Hierarchic radiance operating at the level of perception.

concepts.label: Pure persuasion (seeded)
concepts.gloss: Education dialectically approached has a 'mythic glow' as a form of pure persuasion — the rhetorical motive made ultimate, as in Castiglione's Book IV and Kierkegaard's perpetual courtship.

concepts.label: Attitude (incipient act)
concepts.gloss: Kierkegaard's perpetual courtship — 'renunciation and advance fused in one attitude' — is the clearest instance: a sustained orientation that holds the incipient act in suspension rather than completing it.

concepts.label: Dialectical lyric
concepts.gloss: Burke's characterization of Fear and Trembling: a work performing its argument through feeling-toned dialectical operations (the Kierkegaardian leap) rather than discursive demonstration.

concepts.label: Caricature of courtship
concepts.gloss: The grotesque or fragmentary instantiation of the courtship principle, as in Kafka: formal elements of the paradigm present but distorted; the access-seeker never gains access; mystery intensified by its own opacity.

concepts.label: Hazing and initiation
concepts.gloss: Informal, unacknowledged ritual through which outsiders are tested before admission to a hierarchic group's inner sanctum. The mystery requires initiation rites; their absence produces uncanny suffering without resolution.

concepts.label: Martyrdom as rhetoric
concepts.gloss: Bearing witness before a supermundane audience; the courtier's feats performed in the sovereign's sight. Etymologically from the law courts (witness); epideictic oratory in extremis.

concepts.label: Reversibility of social and religious reverence
concepts.gloss: Structural interchangeability of deference to secular and sacred authority. Social reverence and religious reverence draw sustenance from each other; Castiglione makes it explicit, Kafka grotesque, Kierkegaard dialectical.

concepts.label: Addressed quality
concepts.gloss: Every endowment of the courtier is an endowment of appeal; his prime motive is 'glory,' an essentially addressed motive that lives in the good opinion of others. The courtier's existence is rhetorical in essence.

concepts.label: Kierkegaardian leap
concepts.gloss: The dialectical transformation converting finite contingencies into a vocabulary adequate to the infinite. Burke reads it as a metarhetorical operation: Kierkegaard inserts the principle he needs rather than drawing it out of the Biblical text.

concepts.label: Paradigm vs. caricature
concepts.gloss: Methodological pair: Castiglione as symmetrical, complete, classically resolved instance; Kafka as fragmentary, grotesque, unresolved. Together they mark the range within which the courtship principle actually operates.

concepts.label: Perpetual courtship (Kierkegaard)
concepts.gloss: Kierkegaard's mode of address to Regina after her marriage: courtship in terms of the infinite, in perpetual repetition. The dialectician's motive requires a permanent distance that prevents practical completion.

concepts.label: Grammar of regression
concepts.gloss: Grammatical convertibility whereby logical priority (essence) is stated narratively as temporal priority (childhood, origin). In The Castle: the castle as logical essence appears as childhood memory and imagery.

positions.claim: Courtship is the rhetorical principle operative whenever beings of different social kinds communicate; mystery — the opacity of hierarchic difference — is its ground and its suasive resource.
Sexual and social vocabularies of courtship are interchangeable not because one substitutes for the other but because sexual courtship is intrinsically fused with the motives of social hierarchy.

The socioanagogic sense reads social hierarchy where divine or erotic imagery appears; the poet's symbols glow with hierarchic meaning, as the medievalist was right to detect a hidden realm behind the poet's image.

Castiglione's Book of the Courtier discloses in overt form elements that elsewhere exist only in fragments, making precise the rhetorical convertibility between terms for social hierarchy and terms for theologic hierarchy.

Kafka's Castle is a fragmentary caricature of courtship, showing the principle in Expressionistically grotesque form: bureaucracy as the mystery of 'reverence' without its classical resolution, social mystery serving as an absurdly incommensurate figure for divine mystery.
The absence of discoverable motive intensifies rather than dispels the sense of mystery: once socialized into an opaque system's rules, the very lack of reasons for the mystery adds to it.

Kierkegaard's dialectical operations constitute a metarhetoric of perpetual courtship: renunciation and advance are fused in a single attitude, the finite and infinite reconciled, the incommensurable overcome by the Absurd.

calleja_pim_candidates.rationale: Courtship as rhetoric across social estrangement maps directly onto Shared involvement: guild initiation rituals, mentor-mentee dynamics, elite-player allure, cross-faction social drama all instantiate the mystery/hierarchy structure Burke analyzes.

The courtier's tactical calculations of display, timing, and self-presentation (when to perform feats, how to refuse favors with modesty) map onto tactical micro-decisions within social hierarchies in multiplayer games.

The socioanagogic reading — detecting hierarchic narrative beneath ostensibly erotic or divine surface imagery — maps onto players' construction of social meaning from game-world hierarchies and lore-encoded rank.

interlocutors: Kafka (The Castle, The Trial, Metamorphosis, The Hunger-Artist)
Thomas Mann (Tonio Kroger, Death in Venice, Mario and the Magician)
Freud (children as insects in dreams — footnote)

tensions.description: Mystery requires maintained hierarchic distance for its suasive power, yet rhetoric aims at identification and the closing of that distance — courtship is irreducibly paradoxical: it exploits the gap it simultaneously seeks to bridge.

Castiglione's paradigm (symmetrical, classically resolved, transcendent) vs. Kafka's caricature (grotesque, opaque, unresolvable) — the same principle operates in both, but with opposite aesthetic and existential valences.

The socioanagogic interpreter cannot always know whether social allegory is consciously planted or unconsciously embedded; the identifications can be implicit, the author unaware. This complicates the rhetorical analysis without dissolving it.

Kierkegaard's perpetual courtship: the dialectical resolution (renunciation fused with advance in a single attitude) is formally elegant but existentially costs the elimination of any actual relation — pure persuasion achieved at the price of all finite fulfillment.
